This study examined the relationship between intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation and academic achievement among NCE students of FCT College of Education, Abuja. A correlational survey research design was adopted, as the study sought to determine the extent and direction of the relationship among intrinsic, extrinsic motivation and students’ academic achievement. The population comprised 1,704 NCE II students, from which a sample of 313 students was drawn using the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) table and stratified and simple random sampling techniques was used in selecting the respondents fairly. A total of 311 questionnaires, representing 99.5% of the sampled respondents, were correctly completed and returned. Data were collected using a researcher-developed 30-item structured questionnaire divided into three sections: students’ cumulative grade point average (CGPA), 15 items measuring intrinsic motivation, and 15 items measuring extrinsic motivation. The instrument was face and content validated by experts, yielding a validity index of 0.76, and its reliability was established through a pilot study using Cronbach’s Alpha, which yielded coefficients of 0.93 and 0.88 for intrinsic and extrinsic motivation respectively. Data were analysed using Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed a weak to moderate, positive and significant relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (r = .385, p < .05); a strong, positive and significant relationship between intrinsic motivation and academic achievement (r = .764, p < .05); and a strong, positive and significant relationship between extrinsic motivation and academic achievement (r = .629, p < .05). Consequently, the three null hypotheses were rejected. The study concluded that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are significantly associated with academic achievement. It was recommended that lecturers and school authorities design tasks that are interesting and engaging, employ inquiry-based and student-centred teaching methods, and clearly communicate the career benefits of academic success to enhance student motivation and performance.

Generative artificial intelligence has already forced colleges and universities to rewrite their academic integrity policies. Now it's forcing a harder, equally technical conversation in disability services. Students with documented disabilities are beginning to request generative AI tools as part of their accommodation plans. Many existing accommodation policies do not address these technologies. Campus administrators must address these novel questions now to meet legal obligations under disability law while maintaining their institution's academic standards.

Agentic coding systems increasingly rely on repository-level agent files, such as AGENTS.md, to communicate project knowledge and developer intent. However, it remains unclear which categories of agent instructions enable efficient agent-file generation and accurate code generation. We evaluate five instruction categories: Repository Overview, Function Description, Implementation Detail, Testing, and Reconstruction Steps, across all 31 non-empty combinations using two Large Language Models (LLMs), Gemma 4 and GPT-5.4, and five human-written Python libraries. Our study addresses two research questions, comprising five sub-questions, on agent file generation and code generation. Results show that the number of instructions alone does not determine token usage for agent-file generation, with substantial variation across models and libraries. Although most AI-generated libraries compiled successfully regardless of the instruction combination, functional correctness remained limited. No Gemma 4 variant passed all tests, whereas 12.99% of GPT-5.4 variants did. Function Description achieved Gemma 4's highest partial-pass rate, while Reconstruction Steps achieved GPT-5.4's highest full-pass rate. For structural similarity to human-written code, Reconstruction Steps was most frequently associated with libraries closest to the originals in Lines of File and total Cyclomatic Complexity, while Testing and Reconstruction Steps were jointly most frequent for File Count and Function Count.

This research aims to examine the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing the quality and efficiency of administrative decision-making in Iraq, adopting digital transformation as both an analytical model and an integrated practical framework. The study focuses on the readiness of Iraqi government institutions to adopt intelligent systems and the impact of these technologies on improving decision-making speed and transparency, reducing human error, and fostering a work environment grounded in data and intelligent analysis. The research employs a descriptive-analytical approach to review concepts related to AI and digital transformation, an inductive approach to infer relationships between variables, and a field-based approach involving the analysis of government documents and reports. Content analysis tools were also utilized to assess the extent to which AI applications—such as predictive systems, decision-support algorithms, chatbots, and big data analytics tools—are being employed. The findings indicate that the implementation of AI within Iraqi public administration remains in its early stages, despite official moves toward digitalization. Key opportunities identified include faster decision-making, increased transparency, reduced human intervention in routine tasks, and the creation of reliable databases to support planning and policymaking. Challenges include weak digital infrastructure, limited technical skills among staff, the absence of a legal framework regulating artificial intelligence applications, and poor integration between government systems. The research recommends formulating a comprehensive national strategy for artificial intelligence, developing digital infrastructure, upskilling government personnel, strengthening partnerships with the private sector and academic institutions, and updating legislation to align with digital governance and privacy protection standards, thereby ensuring a secure and effective environment for the adoption of smart technologies.

ABSTRACT Rural transformation - the multidimensional transition of demographic, economic, social, spatial, technological, environmental and institutional conditions in rural areas has traditionally been studied through periodic surveys, census decadal enumeration and retrospective mapping. This paper investigates whether artificial intelligence (AI) can fundamentally transform this analytical paradigm from retrospective description toward continuous, predictive and anticipatory spatio-temporal intelligence. Through a critical synthesis of the emerging GeoAI literature, analysis of primary Indian and international datasets, and development of an original conceptual framework-the AI-Enabled SpatioTemporal Rural Transformation Framework (AI-STRF) this paper argues that AI is not merely improving existing rural research techniques but may be creating a new paradigm of rural geographical analysis. The paper examines AI applications across demographic, agricultural, infrastructural, environmental and socioeconomic dimensions of rural change, identifies critical research gaps, and constructs evidence-based 2030-2050 future scenarios. It concludes that while AI offers transformative potential for predictive rural geography, realisation of this potential depends critically on addressing data inequality, algorithmic bias, institutional capacity, and the fundamental distinction between prediction and causal explanation. The future of rural geography, this paper contends, lies not in replacing human geographical expertise but in augmenting it through intelligent, ethically governed spatio-temporal analysis.

This study investigates how digital leadership and artificial intelligence (AI) contribute to the development of sustainable tourism strategies, focusing on the context of the Turkish hospitality industry. The central research question examines how digital leadership practices guide the strategic use of AI technologies toward sustainability-oriented outcomes. Grounded in digital leadership theory and the triple bottom line sustainability framework, the study adopts a qualitative multiple case study design. Data were collected through document analysis of sustainability reports, strategic plans, and publicly available digital transformation materials from four leading hotel groups in Turkey: Rixos Hotels, Titanic Hotels, Maxx Royal Hotels, and The Marmara Hotels. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and strategic practices. The findings reveal that AI-enabled applications support sustainability by enhancing operational efficiency, enabling personalized service delivery, and improving environmental management practices, particularly in areas such as energy efficiency, resource optimization, and carbon footprint reduction. Furthermore, the results indicate that the alignment of digital leadership with ethical responsibility, innovation orientation, and employee digital capability development strengthens organizational competitiveness and long-term sustainability. The study contributes to the literature by offering an applied strategic framework that conceptualizes digital leadership as a governance mechanism directing AI technologies toward sustainability objectives. Beyond academic contributions, the findings provide practical insights for managers and policymakers seeking to integrate digital transformation initiatives with sustainable tourism strategies, especially in emerging tourism economies.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered music overwhelmingly by way of large industrial models trained on vast corpora, in which the outcome is fixed in advance by an apparatus that the musician neither controls nor understands. This article argues that the essential machine-learning operations of dataset assembly, feature extraction and model fitting can instead be utilised transparently as part of an artist’s creative practice. Looking to David Pye’s concepts of workmanship of certainty and workmanship of risk , this article examines the design of the Tensed Computer Improviser (TCI), an open-source machine improviser built in Max with the Fluid Corpus Manipulation (FluCoMa) toolkit, which trains models from a small audio corpus of the user’s own choosing, with no pretrained component and no external training stage. Situating the TCI within a genealogy of machine improvisation using small data, the article analyses its design through the vocabulary of craft where the corpus curation and training are integrated into the creative act and the characteristic errors of small data are welcomed as tool-marks.

The aim of this study is to examine whether middle school students’ attitudes toward developing Turkish vocabulary differ according to the tools they preferred during the preparation of post-reading presentations. The study employed a quantitative comparative correlational design. The participants consisted of 56 fifth-grade students attending a public middle school in Burhaniye, Balıkesir, Türkiye. Within the framework of the Türkiye Century Education Model, students presented the books they had read by using artificial intelligence-supported tools, conventional digital tools, or hand-prepared materials, based on their own preferences. No intervention was made in the natural learning environment. After the presentations, the Attitude Scale for Developing Vocabulary in the Turkish Course, developed by Yaşar and Topçuoğlu Ünal (2016), was administered. Descriptive statistics and the independent-samples t-test were used for data analysis. The findings revealed that students who preferred artificial intelligence-supported tools obtained significantly higher attitude scores toward developing Turkish vocabulary than those who preferred conventional digital tools or hand-prepared materials. The calculated effect size (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.59) indicated a medium effect. The results suggest that students’ attitudes toward developing Turkish vocabulary differ significantly according to the tools they preferred during the preparation of post-reading presentations.

This study aims to examine the utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and its contribution to strengthening students’ spiritual character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province. The study was motivated by the challenges of providing relevant and engaging Islamic Religious Education for a digitally oriented generation, whose familiarity with technology is not always accompanied by strong spiritual awareness. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. The informants included the Head of the Madrasah, IRE teachers, students, dormitory Ummi, and PMDL administrators. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observations, and documentation of IRE learning activities. The findings indicate that AI was utilized through several applications, including AI-based chatbots to facilitate students’ religious inquiries and spiritual guidance, interactive digital applications to support dhikr and self-reflection (muhasabah), and visual-based AI learning platforms to present Islamic Religious Education materials in a more engaging manner. These applications supported interactive religious learning, encouraged students to reflect on their behavior and religious practices, increased learning motivation, and strengthened emotional engagement with Islamic learning. However, the findings also demonstrate that AI has a supportive rather than substitutive role in spiritual character formation. Teachers remain essential in modeling and cultivating values such as sincerity, patience, discipline, and closeness to Allah SWT through direct guidance and interpersonal interaction. The novelty of this study lies in identifying AI as a complementary pedagogical instrument that connects digital Islamic learning with students’ spiritual self-reflection, while emphasizing the irreplaceable role of teachers in authentic spiritual character formation. This study contributes to the development of technology-integrated Islamic Religious Education by proposing a balanced approach in which AI supports learning innovation without displacing teacher-mediated spiritual formation.

Despite their strengths, Aboriginal mothers experience significant health disparities, including perinatal mental health challenges influenced by social, historical, and cultural determinants. Routine risk screening informs follow-up care, yet conventional approaches often fail to address cultural considerations. The Baby Coming You Ready (BCYR) program provides a strengths-based, culturally adapted digital assessment designed to enhance perinatal mental health care. However, some clinicians continue to rely primarily on conventional risk scores, which can neglect broader contextual circumstances influencing Aboriginal mothers, including cultural strengths and protective factors, thereby limiting the program’s full impact. This exploratory model-development study examined whether generative AI data augmentation combined with an intrinsically interpretable machine-learning model could support culturally contextualised prediction of perinatal psychological distress among Aboriginal mothers. We analysed deidentified BCYR pilot data from 293 Aboriginal mothers across six Western Australian sites. After excluding five records with incomplete outcome data, the analytic dataset included 288 participants. Models were evaluated using repeated internal train-test splits, with synthetic data used only for training augmentation and performance assessed on held-out real test data. The highest internal performance was observed for the TVAE-augmented Explainable Boosting Machine at an augmentation ratio of 1.0, with an accuracy of 0.867, an F1 score of 0.817, and an AUC of 0.934. Model explanations identified self-blame, loneliness, family pride, day-to-day management, sleep, and related contextual factors as influential contributors to model-estimated risk. These explanations are intended as prompts for culturally safe discussion and clinical reflection. Findings suggest that interpretable generative AI may have potential to support culturally responsive perinatal mental health assessment. However, broader community-governed external validation and prospective clinical workflow evaluation are required before clinical implementation.
topics: Maternal Mental Health During Pregnancy and Postpartum

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has made prompting a prominent mode of interaction between users and large language models, but prompting is not exhausted by its technical role in eliciting model outputs. This article proposes Prompt Humanities as an interdisciplinary interpretive framework for examining prompts as rhetorical, hermeneutic, and culturally situated acts. Drawing on philosophical hermeneutics, reader-response criticism, speech-act theory, poststructuralism, Digital Humanities, and postcolonial studies, the framework asks how prompt-mediated interaction reframes questions of interpretation, authorship, dialogue, and knowledge production. The framework is developed through a qualitative close reading of Amitav Ghosh's The Calcutta Chromosome. Rather than claiming that Ghosh predicted contemporary generative AI, the article treats the novel retrospectively as a literary site in which recursive questioning, fragmented archives, distributed forms of knowledge, and computer-mediated inquiry can be compared with prompt-mediated interpretation. The analysis focuses on Murugan's revisionary hypotheses, Mangala's counter-scientific network, Antar's interactions with the digital system Ava, and the novel's persistent resistance to epistemological closure. The article argues that Prompt Humanities can complement existing Digital Humanities and postcolonial approaches by making the prompt itself an object of literary and cultural analysis. Its contribution is therefore not the claim that prompting has been absent from humanities scholarship, but the development of a specific integrative vocabulary for analysing how questions, responses, archives, and interpretive agents are organised in human–AI and literary contexts. The framework is presented as provisional and transferable, requiring further testing across texts, languages, genres, and forms of human–AI interaction.

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to interpret professional situations, formulate arguments, and consider responses to ethical dilemmas. Although these systems can broaden reflection, their persuasive outputs may encourage moral outsourcing, defined as transferring substantive elements of ethical interpretation, justification, or judgment to an external system without adequate examination, endorsement, or responsibility. This conceptual article asks how generative AI can be integrated into philosophical counseling and ethical reflection in teacher education without undermining ethical self-authorship. Drawing on philosophical counseling, moral development, relational autonomy, professional ethics, and AI literacy, it develops the Ethical Self-Authorship Cycle. The model comprises five iterative stages: articulating the dilemma, pluralizing perspectives, interrogating assumptions, testing reasons and consequences, and reclaiming moral authorship. Its contribution is threefold. First, it distributes deliberative functions between the human participant and AI by specifying what the system may contribute and what it cannot establish at each stage. Second, it requires the process to conclude with a human-formulated justification rather than an AI-generated recommendation. Third, it treats ethical self-authorship as a developing capacity requiring pedagogical scaffolding and ethically and digitally prepared teacher educators. An illustrative case demonstrates the model’s application to a dilemma involving student use of AI in assessment. The article argues that AI may generate material for ethical inquiry, but it cannot represent affected people, determine which values should prevail, or assume professional responsibility. Moral authorship and answerability must remain human.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Time-series data generated continuously across industrial, environmental, and especially health domains produce multimodal signals whose scale and heterogeneity make their processing and interpretation particularly challenging. Time-Series Language Models (TSLMs) promise scalable interpretation of these signals, yet remain bottlenecked by a fundamental lack of text-annotated time series pairs that are signal-grounded, reproducible, and extensible across modalities and schemas. Existing paired corpora are either closed or limited in scale and modality coverage. Annotation with large language models could scale them up, but its outputs cannot be regenerated exactly, which prevents others from re-deriving, extending, or auditing the resulting corpus. To address this, we release TimeCap, an open deterministic captioning pipeline with three reusable extractor tiers and a cross-channel synthesis layer that operates directly on the signal with no language model in the loop, extensible to new schemas by writing channel definitions alone. This positions TimeCap as a reproducible mechanism for future dataset generation rather than a one-off release. Applying TimeCap to OpenMHC, the MyHeart Counts wearable dataset, yields MHCap, the largest open caption layer for multimodal wearable time-series data. MHCap spans 19 Apple HealthKit channels and 7,005,763 captions over 908,944 person-days. To showcase the impact of the corpus, we train OpenTSLM, a time-series language model, on MHCap and benchmark on health-outcome prediction. Caption-augmented training (OpenTSLM-Cap) outperforms a label-only baseline on 29 of 32 per-user binary evaluations across 8 tasks.

Abstract This article synthesizes proceedings and outcomes from the 2nd Pracademic Emergency Management and Homeland Security Summit, hosted virtually by Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Worldwide Campus College of Arts & Sciences and its Virtual Collaboratory for Security and Resilience Education, Research, and Engagement. Drawing on contributions from an international and interdisciplinary group of scholars, practitioners, students, policymakers, and professional organizations representing higher education, government, industry, and operational practice, the summit examined emerging challenges and future directions across homeland security, emergency management, resilience, public health, homeland defense, disaster planning, information disorder, artificial intelligence, ethics, and standards development. Several cross-cutting findings emerged. First, preparedness and resilience increasingly require adaptive, inclusive, and whole-community approaches grounded in trusted communication, social capital, functional needs inclusion, and meaningful stakeholder engagement. Second, while artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and advanced decision-support systems offer substantial operational promise, their implementation demands stronger attention to ethical oversight, interoperability, governance, and consensus-based standards capable of translating technical capability into operational relevance. Third, increasingly complex threat environments reinforce the need for critical thinking, scenario-based learning, ethical reasoning, and career-long professional development to prepare leaders to operate across institutional boundaries and under incomplete information.

Architectural education is a field that uniquely targets the creativity and continuous development of architecture students. This is especially true within environmental architecture, which relies on diverse spatial and temporal variables that create unique interactions for students, based on the specific concept of environmental design.

Background The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has created an ontological disruption in higher education, challenging traditional pedagogical mediation and academic production. This study examines the transformation of the teaching role in university environments across Peru, Chile, and Colombia, addressing a knowledge gap in Latin American empirical research regarding faculty perceptions and daily practices with Large Language Models. Methods The research employed a descriptive-interpretative qualitative design with an open-ended survey approach interpreted through a hermeneutic lens. A non-probabilistic sample of 48 undergraduate and graduate professors from 20 Higher Education Institutions in the region participated. Data were collected through a validated 18-item structured online questionnaire and analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis assisted by Atlas.ti software. Results The findings identify a transition from traditional instructional roles toward a “mediator-curator” model, where educators act as orchestrators of human-AI co-intelligence. Key applications include pedagogical re-engineering, such as dynamic curricular design, Socratic tutoring, and the shift from product-oriented to process-oriented assessment. Critical dimensions emerged regarding the need for pedagogical re-engineering, ethical challenges in academic integrity, and the development of critical AI literacy. National variations showed Chile focusing on pedagogical equity, Colombia on research productivity, and Peru on didactic agility. Conclusions The integration of GenAI in the Latin American university context requires a situated pedagogical response that transcends instrumental use. The study proposes a new learning ecology where the teacher facilitates critical interaction between students and generative systems. This shift necessitates a reconfiguration of teaching competencies toward epistemic curation and algorithmic responsibility to ensure meaningful and ethical learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.

Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diversity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8's and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the ideas, our model's success@k is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8's, so we see that the added diversity does not cost any executability.

Large language models rely on spurious features in clinical classification: swapping a single gender token in clinical notes alters gender-irrelevant diagnoses in up to 53.5% of cases. Existing inference-time corrections either need counterfactual data built around the specific spurious feature or behave unpredictably. We observe that how a model's preference between answers evolves across layers, its prediction trajectory, indicates for each document whether a correction is likely to help. We propose Trajectory-Guided Steering (TGS), which decides from the trajectory alone whether to correct each prediction and in which direction, with no counterfactual data and no knowledge of the spurious feature. On 16 clinical classification tasks from i2b2, TGS fixes 17.7% of errors while breaking only 1.3% of correct predictions and stays net-positive across all tested hyperparameter settings; all baselines are net-negative or near zero. The same corrections reduce reliance on the spurious feature: on the most affected diseases, gender-swap inconsistency falls sharply (hypertension 53.5% -> 38.0%, diabetes 35.1% -> 21.5%). Applying the correction to every document instead raises breaks on correct positive predictions from 0.1% to 6.4%, so per-document selection is essential. TGS also transfers to three model families and three other clinical and biomedical datasets.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Accurate estimation of cancer risk from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) could support earlier detection and improved care, but modeling such complex patient trajectories remains challenging. We present TrajOnco, a training-free, multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework designed for scalable multi-cancer early detection. Using a chain-of-agents architecture with long-term memory, TrajOnco performs temporal reasoning over sequential clinical events to generate patient-level summaries, evidence-linked rationales, and predicted risk scores. We evaluated TrajOnco on de-identified Truveta EHR data across 15 cancer types using matched case-control cohorts, predicting risk of cancer diagnosis at 1 year. In zero-shot evaluation, TrajOnco achieved AUROCs of 0.64–0.80, performing comparably to supervised machine learning in a lung cancer benchmark while demonstrating better temporal reasoning than single-agent LLMs. The multi-agent design also enabled effective temporal reasoning with smaller-capacity models such as GPT-4.1-mini. The groundedness of TrajOnco’s output was supported by human evaluation. Furthermore, TrajOnco’s interpretable reasoning outputs can be aggregated to reveal population-level risk patterns that align with established clinical knowledge. These findings highlight the potential of multi-agent LLMs to execute interpretable temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHRs, advancing both scalable multi-cancer early detection and clinical insight generation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a major technological force in the modern knowledge system. AI is transforming the way knowledge is discovered, organized, analyzed, disseminated, and preserved. Academic libraries in higher education are also an important part of this transformation. Technologies such as generative AI, intelligent information retrieval systems, AI-based chatbots, automated metadata generation, and digital repositories can make library services more efficient and user-centric. However, the use of AI has also created challenges such as information accuracy, data privacy, copyright, intellectual property, plagiarism, algorithmic bias, and digital inequality. Therefore, it is necessary to use AI in an ethical, safe, transparent, and human-centered manner, not just as a technological advancement. UNESCO (2023) has emphasized the importance of a human-centered approach, data privacy, and inclusion in the use of generative AI in education and research. This article has done a conceptual study of AI, higher education, National Education Policy 2020, open knowledge, information ethics, research integrity and inclusive library services. Based on this study, the concept of 'Human-Centric AI Library Ecosystem' has been proposed. Its main pillars are intelligent information search, open knowledge infrastructure, research integrity, ethical data management, inclusive access and continuous skill development of librarians.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) in educational technology has opened new opportunities for enhancing constructivist learning, particularly in computer network education. This study aimed to design, develop, and evaluate Comnet-Art, an AI-based AR learning application, to improve students' understanding and constructivist skills in computer networks. The research involved 234 undergraduate students and employed the ADDIE model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) along with expert validation, practicality testing, and effectiveness assessment. Validation results indicated strong content and media validity, with average Aiken's V scores of 0.92 from media experts and 0.89 from material experts, categorized as very valid. Practicality assessments revealed high usability and engagement, with educators reporting an average practicality score of 91.85% and students 90.71%. Effectiveness evaluation using pre-test and post-test comparisons demonstrated substantial learning gains, with the mean score increasing from 68.21 to 86.47 and a relative improvement of 26.76%, confirming the application's effectiveness in fostering engagement, collaboration, problem-solving, and constructivist learning outcomes. These findings highlight that Comnet-Art successfully integrates AI-driven interactivity and AR visualization to support active learning, improve conceptual understanding, and enhance higher-order cognitive skills. This study provides strong evidence that emerging technologies such as AI and AR can be effectively leveraged to transform engineering education and promote constructivist learning.

This chapter explores the impacts of technological innovation on workplace culture and new opportunities for women in the workplace. It highlights how the rapid uptake of digital technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), cloud computing, and automation affect the work system, decision-making process, and engagement. Technology allows women to diminish bias in recruitment and employee evaluation, enhance leadership opportunities, and create a work-life balance. But there are challenges, such as algorithmic bias, the digital gender divide, and cultural barriers in patriarchal organizations. This chapter uses a model that illustrates the impact of technology on work culture. It shows that technology can only empower women if there is gender-sensitive policy, a commitment from organizations, and digital literacy. It suggests that organizations need to combine technology adoption with inclusive policies and systems, mentoring, and flexible working to drive business transformation. Organizations can build a more empowering digital space for women through the synergy between technology and cultural and structural reform.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education through changes in teaching, research, student support, administrative coordination, data-driven decision-making, and academic evaluation. In Kazakhstan, these changes are especially significant because higher education has been positioned as a strategic pillar of modernization, competitiveness, and human capital development since the Kazakhstan 2050 agenda. At the same time, the literature shows a persistent tension between women’s strong participation in tertiary education and their weaker representation in STEM-intensive pathways, digital leadership, and senior decision-making positions. This article argues that the impact of AI on higher education in Kazakhstan should not be evaluated solely in terms of technological adoption or institutional efficiency but also in terms of how it transforms workplace culture for women. Based on a narrative review of recent academic and policy literature, the chapter examines how AI intersects with academic work, institutional culture, women’s participation, STEM persistence, and leadership in Kazakhstani universities. It proposes a conceptual framework linking national modernization, AI affordances, mediating institutional conditions, and workplace culture mechanisms to women’s outcomes in higher education. The chapter concludes that AI can support a more inclusive and future-oriented higher education system only when universities align technological innovation with gender-inclusive governance, digital capability development, fair recognition systems, and supportive organizational cultures.

Panchakarma is a key element of Ayurvedic medicine with proven benefits for prevention and treatment. Various Panchakarma procedures rely on the skill, physical strength and consistency of the therapists. Variations in the way therapists perform their manual techniques can affect the clinical outcome of the treatment being provided. The introduction of automation and robotics into the practice of Panchakarma is a new avenue that has the potential to address these limitations; offering greater precision, reproducibility, safety and operational efficiency. Some examples of possible innovations include robotic massage systems that can replicate the standardized massage techniques used in Ayurveda, automated massage tables that are equipped for Swedana therapies such as Pottali Swedana, AI (Artificial Intelligence) driven dispensing systems that can provide controlled dosing of oil to the patient during Abhyanga treatments, and sensor-laden monitoring systems that can continuously monitor the physiological parameters of the patient and allow for real-time modification of their treatment. Integration of AI with conventional Panchakarma can help in maintaining the authenticity of Ayurvedic therapies while improving standardization, accessibility, scalability and quality of care. This can help in modernizing Panchakarma without losing its basic therapeutic principles.. 1, Dr 2

documents.abstract: Recent multilingual large language models achieve strong translation performance, yet the internal mechanisms responsible for low-resource multilingual translation remain insufficiently understood. In this paper, we study translation circuits in multilingual decoder-only LLMs for Hindi-to-Urdu and Hindi-to-Sindhi (Devanagari). We propose TITAN, a mechanistic framework that combines causal intervention, sparse feature decomposition, and targeted preference optimization to identify and optimize crucial translation components in the transformer. Unlike conventional full-parameter fine-tuning, TITAN restricts optimization to sparse, causally important circuits, enabling scalable and parameter-efficient adaptation while updating fewer than 5% of model parameters. Experimental results show that TITAN achieves BLEU improvements of 33.75% on Hindi-to-Urdu and 45.86% on Hindi-to-Sindhi over the strongest multilingual baselines. Human expert evaluation further confirms substantial gains in adequacy and fluency across both language pairs. Additional analyses reveal that multilingual translation is implemented through sparse, structured circuits operating over a shared semantic subspace rather than through an English-centric pivot representation. Overall, our findings demonstrate that mechanistic circuit discovery can directly improve low-resource multilingual translation while providing interpretable insights into multilingual transformer behavior.

Reliable 3D person detection is important for rescue robotics to give first responders situational awareness. Yet most multimodal 3D detection research targets automotive scenarios in which pedestrians mostly appear in a narrow range of upright, near-road poses. It is therefore unclear how much of the reported performance transfers to rescue settings, as a person may be lying, partially occluded, or in unstructured indoor and outdoor environments. To investigate this gap, we introduce TriSAR-3D, a multimodal person detection dataset recorded with a high-resolution 128-channel LiDAR, an RGB camera, and a thermal camera. It captures varied poses in indoor as well as outdoor locations at different times of day to study their influence on 3D object detector performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel trimodal 3D detection pipeline, PaintFusion, that fuses PointPainting-based evidence using a simple MLP. We show that the derived method reaches 65.4 AP@50 and thereby outperforms strong LiDAR-only (CenterPoint, 53.4), RGB+LiDAR (BEVFusion, 60.5), and adapted trimodal (Tri-BEVFusion, 60.7) baselines on the dataset. At the same time, it is substantially faster than other fusion-based methods such as BEVFusion, with a per-frame latency of 51.6 ms compared to 101 ms. Additionally, we test how the performance of different 3D object detectors generalizes to unseen pose categories. Removing lying instances from training data collapses the lying-pose AP@50 to near zero across all evaluated detectors. The results indicate that dataset diversity exerts a large effect on 3D object detection performance. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/MarkusKramer1/3D-Trimodal-People-Detection.

Context: Generative-AI coding assistants have moved rapidly into software development practice, raising human-factor questions about trust, usability, and responsible adoption that lab studies and surveys do not fully answer; sustained turn-by-turn production traces remain rare. Objective: This study examines four human-factor dimensions of sustained generative-AI-assisted development — trust calibration, developer gating, delegation-related prompt dynamics, and authorial identity — in a real production setting. Methods: Longitudinal autoethnography of a 16-month single-developer construction of a cloud-native institutional service at a Taiwanese university (424 git commits, Dec 2024 – Apr 2026), with two prompt corpora across two IDE-mediated assistants used in succession: 172 user prompts plus 2777 assistant turns from Cursor IDE (Sep–Dec 2025), and 50 user prompts from Claude Code CLI (Apr 2026). Per-session formal indicators (Eqs. (1) , (2) , (3) , (4) , (5) ), an analysis of a pre-stated directional prediction (Section 5.3 ), and triangulation with a companion architectural analysis (Chi, 2026) constrain interpretation. Results: (T) Trust calibration — in the trace-documented stuck-loop episode, the developer escalated model tier rather than revising specification (a capacity-oriented escalation). (G) Gating — the agent iteration ratio rises with task ambiguity, consistent with reduced developer gating of the agent loop when prompting is under-specified. (D) Delegation — within the Cursor window, prompt length compresses by up to 98.7% within a session (first to last third) while rewrite signals do not consistently decline, and prompt-skill improvement is not measurable under the study’s indicators, a pattern interpreted as consistent with a shift from prompting toward delegation rather than a direct measurement of it; in the later Claude Code window, 33 of 50 prompts are follow-ups (66%), a cross-tool observation reported descriptively. (I) Identity diffusion — authoring voice in commit messages converges toward the assistant’s register. Conclusion: Engineering throughput appeared to decouple from the developer-side communication indicators across the period; potential developer-side effects of sustained AI assistance may not register in conventional engineering metrics, supporting a cautionary reading for human-factor-aware adoption. All quantitative magnitudes reported are observations from one case; the four dimensions are offered for analytical generalization, as hypotheses for multi-developer studies to test, not as evidence of general developer behaviour. The article closes with responsible-adoption implications for IDE-assistant design.

The exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cloud computing technologies has revolutionized data processing and intelligent service delivery at scale. Organizations across virtually every sector now rely on cloud-hosted machine learning pipelines to extract value from data that is collected continuously, at volumes and velocities that on-premises infrastructure struggles to match. However, this technological advancement comes with significant challenges, particularly concerning privacy and security of sensitive data transmitted to cloud environments. This research paper addresses the critical intersection of trustworthy cloud infrastructure and privacy-preserving artificial intelligence processing. Our work explores a comprehensive framework that integrates privacy protection mechanisms, secure computation techniques, and confidence assessment measures to establish reliable and trustworthy AI services in cloud environments. We propose that by combining differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, and confidence-aware prediction mechanisms, organizations can maintain data confidentiality while leveraging the computational power of cloud-based AI systems. Rather than treating privacy, security, and reliability as separate concerns to be bolted onto a finished system, the framework proposed here treats them as first-class design requirements that shape every layer of the processing pipeline, from data ingestion through model inference to the communication of results back to end users. This study examines existing privacy-preserving techniques applicable to cloud AI, analyzes their performance trade-offs, and evaluates the reliability of AI predictions through confidence scoring. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to achieve a balanced approach where sensitive data remains protected, AI model performance remains acceptable, and computational overhead is manageable. The research contributes to the development of secure, trustworthy AI solutions suitable for healthcare, financial services, educational institutions, and other sectors requiring stringent privacy compliance. We further situate our contribution within the broader movement toward trustworthy and responsible AI, arguing that privacy-preservation is not merely a compliance checkbox but a foundational property that determines whether AI systems can be adopted at scale in sensitive domains.

Test-time scaling can improve the performance of large language models by generating multiple answers to a question and aggregating them. Weighted ensembles extend this idea by drawing answers from several models, with the weights determining how often each model is used. Learning these weights from a training dataset involves two sample sizes: $Q$ labeled questions and $N$ generations per model and question. We study their interplay through the clean risk, the population error of the ensemble's infinite-generation voting rule. Under a margin condition with exponent $β$, we show that empirical risk minimization (ERM) with a calibrated margin buffer achieves excess risk of order $Q^{-1/2}+N^{-β/2}$, up to logarithmic factors, for fixed numbers of models and candidate answers. To investigate the optimality of this dependence on $Q$ and $N$, we analyze a simplified submodel with two models and two possible answers per question. We characterize its minimax excess risk up to constants by a Hellinger modulus for a binomial-mixture experiment. Polynomial approximation and spectral analysis reveal three regimes. When questions are relatively scarce, the $Q^{-1/2}$ term governs learning and the general buffered ERM is optimal. In an intermediate regime, pooling generation counts across questions improves upon estimating each answer distribution separately, with only logarithmic gains from additional questions. With sufficiently many questions, the minimax excess risk reaches an $N^{-β}$ identification floor that persists even with infinitely many questions. The submodel's lower bounds also apply to general ensembles, matching the buffered-ERM upper bound up to logarithmic factors when questions are scarce and in parts of the intermediate regime. Questions remain about the transitions between regimes and the construction of matching pooled estimators for general ensembles.

Today, it is seen that artificial intelligence technology is used in the field of education as well as in many other fields, and it is thought that artificial intelligence tools can also be used in recreation education at the higher education level. This study, prepared in line with this idea, has been conducted to determine the areas of use of artificial intelligence tools in recreation education at the higher education level and their potential contributions to this education. The study has been designed according to the case study approach, one of the qualitative research designs, and the data necessary to achieve the purpose of the study have been collected through the interview technique. The interview has been conducted with ChatGPT, one of the chatbots, and 8 questions have been asked to this robot. Data obtained from the ChatGPT interview has been subjected to descriptive analysis. From the analysis, it has been found that artificial intelligence tools support the course environment in terms of individual follow-up and success of students through personalized education. In addition to this finding, it has been understood that the use of artificial intelligence in recreation education can enable the creation of location-independent courses with simulation and augmented reality tools and provide students with real-life experience. Therefore, the study concludes that the use of artificial intelligence has a positive effect on the education process of recreation students and will contribute to the training of more qualified personnel for the sector.

SignificanceComplex drug products remain costly and inaccessible to many patients. The use of modern imaging technologies offers transformative tools to address generic drug research challenges, allowing for improved patient access to safe and effective generic medicines.AimThis review summarizes imaging research related to a wide range of complex drug products across five coordinated initiatives: high-order characterization of the arrangement of matter in complex products; elucidation of the relationship between the structural features and the functional performance of these dosage forms; establishment of noninvasive approaches to characterize and compare the rate and extent of drug bioavailability from these dosage forms; development of reliable artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches to analyze imaging data; and provision of mechanistic insights to inform the construction of computational models.Results and ConclusionsThe technologies summarized in this work enabled non-destructive structural characterization of complex drug products, establishment of structure-performance relationships, and direct measurement of drug availability at local sites of action. Furthermore, currently available technologies used for imaging complex drug products continue to support the establishment of scientifically rigorous, efficient bioequivalence pathways for complex generic products, reducing reliance on costly comparative clinical endpoint studies.
